thesis.title: Lexicon and Allocation
thesis.thesis: Training on human reports explains a model's self-report lexicon: which predicates it uses and how they are phrased. It does not explain allocation: which particular episodes receive which predicates. Evidence about the model's internal states lives in allocation.
thesis.argument_sketch: Human training data fixes the repertoire, such as 'I'm unsure', 'this is confusing' and 'I'm not certain I remember'. But the corpus does not say on which of the model's own forward passes to deploy each phrase. When allocation covaries with independently measured internal variables beyond what surface features of the prompt predict, the covariance needs a mechanism, and the training story alone does not supply one. Examples of such variables are output entropy, retrieval failure and activation of particular features. A properly controlled test regresses report allocation on internal variables while holding prompt-level predictors fixed. This dissolves the dilemma 'trained or tracking?': a report can be trained in its lexicon and tracking in its allocation.
thesis.why_new: Existing calibration work (e.g., on LLM confidence) and the philosophical literature do not separate these two explananda. The distinction identifies exactly which component of a report the training explanation can and cannot screen off.

objection.objection: The lexicon/allocation split is false for a next-token predictor, so the argument's central premise fails. Training does not just fix a repertoire. It fits the conditional distribution P(report | context), and that distribution already includes allocation. Human corpora encode when humans say 'I'm unsure': on obscure, ambiguous or rare-entity questions. The model's internal variables are not independent of this. Output entropy and retrieval failure are themselves learned functions of the same input and are largely driven by the same corpus statistics, such as the training frequency of the queried fact. So corpus frequency is a common cause of both the internal variable and the imitated hedge. Post-training then supplies exactly the mechanism the argument says is missing. RLHF, honesty fine-tuning and calibration training reward hedging on the model's own errors, so they train allocation directly on the model's forward passes. The proposed regression cannot separate the hypotheses either. Internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt. If 'prompt-level predictors' means the full prompt, the internal variables have no residual variance to explain. If it means a hand-picked set of surface features, residual covariance is guaranteed for any network whose representations are richer than those features. Either way, a positive result is predicted by 'trained, not tracking'. The dilemma is not dissolved; it reappears at the level of allocation.
objection.rationale: This attacks the load-bearing inference: that covariance beyond surface predictors 'needs a mechanism the training story does not supply.' Training supplies one at two levels. Pretraining imitates human allocation, which correlates with the model's uncertainty through shared causes. Fine-tuning shapes allocation explicitly on the model's own outputs. Kadavath et al. (2022) already show calibrated self-evaluation emerging this way. The objection also shows that the proposed observational test is confounded by construction, so the argument has no clean evidential route. It falls short of fatal (5) because the core intuition can be rebuilt. One step is to drop the 'training vs. tracking' contrast and define tracking as counterfactual causal dependence of report allocation on an internal variable, whatever its training origin. Training can then be the source of a tracking mechanism rather than a rival to it. The other step is to replace regression with intervention. Examples are activation steering or concept injection, as in Lindsey et al. (2025) on introspective awareness, where the internal state is manipulated while the prompt is held exactly fixed. Allocation evidence then counts only if reports follow the manipulated state where the corpus prior and the prompt would predict otherwise. As written, the thesis's main premise and its proposed method both fail. The repair is substantial, so the paper's central argument would have to change.

closest_work.work: Comșa & Shanahan (2025), 'Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?' (arXiv:2506.05068)
closest_work.relation: Closest philosophical statement. They propose a 'lightweight' criterion: a self-report is introspective when it is causally connected to the internal state it describes, and not merely a human-mimicking string. Their contrast between an LLM's 'creative process' report (mimicry) and its temperature self-estimate (causally grounded) is essentially your lexicon/allocation split, without the regression design.

closest_work.work: Song, Hu & Mahowald (2025), 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language' (arXiv:2503.07513)
closest_work.relation: Runs nearly your proposed test. It asks whether a model's metalinguistic reports predict its own internal string probabilities better than a near-identical model's internals do. That control, partialling out what any similarly trained system would say, is a stronger version of 'hold prompt-level predictors fixed'. Its result is negative, which bears directly on your empirical bet.

closest_work.work: Binder et al. (2024/ICLR 2025), 'Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection'
closest_work.relation: Operationalizes 'beyond surface features': model A predicts its own behavior better than model B, even though B was fine-tuned on A's behavior. This is the self-vs-observer privileged-access control your argument needs.

closest_work.work: Lindsey (2025), 'Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models' (Transformer Circuits)
closest_work.relation: Goes further than your design. It intervenes on feature activations through concept injection and checks whether the reports follow, which supplies the causal mechanism your covariance-only design leaves open.

closest_work.work: Kadavath et al. (2022), 'Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know'; Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022), 'Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words'; Ji-An et al. (2025), 'Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations'
closest_work.relation: Empirical precursors on allocation. Lin et al. explicitly ask whether verbalized calibration is more than imitation of human uncertainty talk. Kadavath et al. show P(IK)-style reports track correctness. Ji-An et al. test whether reports track projections of internal activations.

closest_work.work: Long (2023), 'Introspective Capabilities in Large Language Models' (JCS 30(9–10)); Perez & Long (2023), 'Towards Evaluating AI Systems for Moral Status Using Self-Reports'
closest_work.relation: Philosophical framing of the trained-vs-introspective problem. They propose validating self-reports on questions with independently checkable answers, i.e. checking allocation against ground truth.

closest_work.work: Maniscalco & Lau (2012), meta-d′; Fleming & Lau (2014), 'How to Measure Metacognition'; Nisbett & Wilson (1977)
closest_work.relation: Human-science ancestors of the core move. Type-2 signal detection already separates metacognitive bias (how confidence words are used overall) from metacognitive sensitivity (whether they are allocated to the right trials). Nisbett & Wilson's actor/observer comparison is the original 'beyond what an outsider with the stimulus could predict' control.

novelty.note:
The slogan 'trained in lexicon, tracking in allocation' and its explicit use to dissolve the trained-or-tracking dilemma is a tidy formulation I have not seen stated in exactly those words. The underlying argument and the test design, however, are substantially in the literature above, especially Comșa & Shanahan, Song et al., Binder et al. and Lindsey. The bias/sensitivity distinction from type-2 SDT is the same conceptual cut. A referee would ask for these to be cited and for the paper's contribution to be narrowed.

The argument also has three weaknesses as stated.

(1) The premise that training does not explain allocation is false for post-trained models. Honesty and calibration fine-tuning, RLHF penalties on confident errors, and Kadavath-style P(IK) training directly shape which episodes receive 'I'm unsure'. Pretraining also teaches the conditional distribution of hedges given context. So training supplies a candidate mechanism for allocation, not only for lexicon. The dilemma is not dissolved; it is relocated to allocation.

(2) Residual covariance with entropy or feature activation does not establish tracking in any self-monitoring sense. A common-cause model fits the same data: a 'hard or unfamiliar input' representation drives both high entropy and the token 'unsure', with no state being monitored. This is the gap between Comșa & Shanahan's lightweight causal criterion and a metarepresentational criterion. You need to say which one 'tracking' means and why your evidence discriminates between them. Covariance alone cannot; interventions in the style of Lindsey, plus dissociation tests, are required.

(3) 'Holding prompt-level predictors fixed' is underspecified. Every internal variable is a deterministic function of the prompt, so the residual depends entirely on which predictor set you choose. Song et al.'s answer is to use a sibling model's internals as the observer baseline. Without a principled observer baseline, the regression can be made to show tracking or no tracking at will.

# Trained in Lexicon, Keyed in Allocation: Language-Model Self-Reports and the Common-Cause Objection

## 1. The dilemma and a proposal

Large language models produce sentences such as "I'm not sure," "this is confusing," and "I'm not certain I remember." These are self-reports in grammatical form. The question is whether they are evidence about the internal states of the system that produces them.

A familiar worry says they are not. The models are trained on enormous corpora of human self-reports, so they would produce such sentences whether or not anything inside them corresponds to what the sentences describe. Birch (2024) calls the general version of this the *gaming problem*: behavioural markers that would be evidence of a state in an animal lose their evidential force in a system optimized to reproduce those markers. Perez and Long (2023) make a parallel point about self-reports specifically. The worry is usually posed as a dilemma. Either a model's report is *trained*, and so evidentially idle, or it is *tracking*, and so evidence of the state it reports. Since every report a model produces is trained in some sense, the dilemma seems to resolve in the deflationist's favour.

The proposal I defend splits self-report behaviour into two components.

- **Lexicon** is the repertoire of predicates a model uses and their phrasing.
- **Allocation** is the mapping from particular episodes to particular predicates: which forward passes are followed by "I'm unsure" and which are not.

Training on human reports clearly explains the lexicon. The proposal is that it does not explain allocation. Allocation is where evidence about internal states lives. Suppose allocation covaries with independently measured internal variables, such as output entropy, retrieval failure, or the activation of particular features, beyond what prompt-level predictors explain. Then that covariance needs a mechanism, and imitation of humans does not supply one. A report can be trained in its lexicon and tracking in its allocation, so the dilemma dissolves.

## 2. The Common-Cause Objection

A strong objection says this proposal fails at its central premise. It has four parts.

1. **No split.** A next-token predictor is not given a repertoire and then left to allocate it. Training fits the whole conditional distribution P(report | context), and that distribution already encodes allocation. Human corpora record *when* people say "I'm unsure": on obscure questions, ambiguous questions, and questions about rare entities.
2. **Common cause.** The model's internal variables are not independent of this. Entropy and retrieval failure are learned functions of the same inputs, driven by the same corpus statistics, notably how often the queried fact appears in training (Kandpal et al. 2023). Corpus frequency is therefore a common cause of the internal variable and of the imitated hedge.
3. **Post-training supplies the mechanism.** Reinforcement learning from human feedback, honesty fine-tuning, and calibration training (e.g. Lin, Hilton and Evans 2022) reward hedging on the model's own errors. They train allocation directly on the model's forward passes, so the "missing mechanism" is not missing.
4. **The test cannot discriminate.** Internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt.
   - If "prompt-level predictors" means the full prompt, the internal variables have no residual variance left to explain anything.
   - If it means a hand-picked set of surface features, residual covariance is guaranteed for any network whose representations are richer than those features.
   - Either way, a positive result is predicted by "trained, not tracking." The dilemma reappears at the level of allocation.

I think the objection is right about several things, and I concede them below:

- The proposal as first stated overstates what the corpus fails to fix.
- The regression design as first stated is inadequate.
- Post-training does supply a mechanism.

But the objection's conclusion does not follow. Properly developed, the objection's own premises sharpen the original idea rather than refute it.

The revised thesis I will argue for is this. Training on human reports explains the lexicon and one specific component of allocation, which I call *inherited allocation*. Evidence about internal states lives in a different component: the counterfactual dependence of allocation on model-specific variables once inherited allocation is held fixed. That dependence is identified by comparative and interventional designs, not by observational regression within a single network. Its aetiology, including post-training on the model's own errors, does not compete with its evidential import. The question "trained or tracking?" is replaced by a question about *causal grain*. That question has more than two answers, and they can be told apart.

## 3. What the corpus fixes: inherited allocation

Start with part (1). The objector is right that pretraining fits a conditional distribution that includes something deserving the name "allocation." The question is *which* allocation, and the answer follows from what a human corpus records.

**What the corpus records.** Consider contexts x in which a speaker is asked something and may hedge. The process that generates the human corpus D involves three things:

- the context x;
- the epistemic state s of the human author who confronts x;
- the report r the author produces.

Only x and r are written down. The author's state is not.

**What pretraining converges to.** A model trained to optimality on D therefore converges toward

> P_D(r | x) = Σ_s P_D(r | x, s) · P_D(s | x).

This expression has two features that matter.

1. It is a function of x alone.
2. Its dependence on x runs through P_D(s | x), the probability that a typical author confronting x is in a hedging state.

Call A_D(x) = P_D(hedge | x) the *inherited allocation*. It is the hedge rate appropriate to the population of human authors who might have written a continuation of x. The objector is right that the corpus fixes A_D. The objector is also right that A_D correlates with obscurity, ambiguity, and rarity, since those are what put human authors into hedging states.

**What the corpus leaves out.** The model's own state never appears in this derivation. Call that state m: for a factual query, whether the relevant attribute is actually retrieved in the model's forward pass. The corpus contains no term for m. So inherited allocation is not allocation over the model's forward passes in the sense my proposal needed. It is allocation over *prompts*, at the rate fitting a typical human. Two systems with identical A_D but different competence profiles would, as pure imitators, hedge identically. One of them would then hedge on things it knows, and the other would answer confidently things it does not know.

So the lexicon/allocation split survives, in a refined form. The corpus determines the lexicon and A_D. It does not determine whether, and how, reports depend on m beyond their dependence on x. The original claim that "the corpus does not say on which of the model's own forward passes to deploy each phrase" was too quick: the corpus says a great deal about when to deploy each phrase, but only for a typical human author. The correct claim is narrower. Whatever the corpus says about allocation, it says through A_D.

**A twist in the objector's favour, which turns out not to be.** Pretraining could itself make reports depend on m. A model trying to predict whether a human author would hedge on x needs an estimate of how obscure x is. One excellent cue to obscurity is the model's own difficulty in answering. If retrieval fails, the fact is probably rare, and a human writing about it probably hedged. A good imitator therefore has reason to use m as an input to its hedge prediction.

This looks like grist for the objector: a purely imitative objective can wire the internal variable into the hedge. But consider what it implies.

- If pretraining makes r depend on m, then r *does* carry information about m, even though the system was optimized to predict humans, not to report on itself.
- It also makes a distinctive prediction. On items where human obscurity and model competence come apart, such a system will follow m. It will be a *worse* imitator of humans and a *better* indicator of itself.

The twist therefore does not support "trained, not tracking." It shows that the training objective does not settle what the report depends on. That brings us to the issue on which the whole debate turns.

## 4. Aetiology is not grain

The dilemma "trained or tracking?" treats the two options as rivals. They are rivals only if the fact that a reporting disposition was produced by training excludes, or undercuts, its counterfactual dependence on the state reported. Nothing supports that assumption.

**What evidence requires.** A report is evidence about a state to the extent that observing it should change our credence about the state. It is robust evidence to the extent that the report counterfactually depends on the state, so that intervening on the state would change the report (Dretske 1981; Woodward 2003). Facts about *why* this dependence exists, such as an engineer's calibration, natural selection, or a gradient, do not cancel the dependence. Two examples make the point.

- **The thermometer.** A thermometer calibrated against a reference instrument is not shown to be untrustworthy by the discovery that it was calibrated. Calibration is what makes it trustworthy.
- **The child.** A child learns to say "I don't know" from caregivers who respond to the child's actual performance. The caregivers praise honest admissions and correct confident errors. That is, structurally, post-training on the learner's own errors. No one infers that the child's "I don't know" is trained and therefore not tracking. The training explains how the tracking was installed.

**What this does to part (3) of the objection.** Post-training that rewards hedging on the model's own errors does supply a mechanism for allocation. But it is not the mechanism my proposal denied the corpus could supply. The proposal concerned training on *human* reports. Post-training on the model's own errors is a different process, and it is precisely the kind of process that installs dependence on the model's own states. A reward that depends on the model's own correctness can only be maximized by a policy whose reports depend on something correlated with its own correctness. That something is either the state that determines correctness or a proxy for it.

So the objection's third part is not a defeater. It is a candidate *explanation* of tracking. The proposal should have said so from the start.

**Separating calibration from resolution.** The post-training point does have a residue worth keeping. Some post-training effects do not touch allocation at all. A reward model that prefers hedged prose shifts the *base rate* of hedging. Such a shift can improve aggregate calibration while leaving the item-by-item pattern of hedges unchanged.

The forecasting literature has the right tools here. Murphy (1973) decomposed the probability score into three parts:

- **reliability**, the match between stated confidence and observed frequency;
- **resolution**, the ability to give different forecasts on occasions with different outcomes;
- **uncertainty**, the base-rate difficulty of the task.

A forecaster who always predicts the base rate is perfectly calibrated and has zero resolution. Allocation evidence is a matter of resolution, not calibration. A model's overall hedge rate is a lexical-stylistic fact. Its *discrimination* between the episodes it gets right and the episodes it gets wrong is the allocation fact.

**The real question.** Once aetiology is separated from dependence, "trained, not tracking" cannot simply mean "this was produced by training." It must be a claim about causal grain: the claim that allocation is keyed to variables *other than* the state the report is taken to be about. That is a substantive empirical hypothesis. It comes in several versions, and they make different predictions.

## 5. Four hypotheses about causal grain

Fix a class of reports, say expressions of uncertainty about factual queries. Distinguish three kinds of variable the report might depend on.

- **m\*** is the *first-order variable*: the internal variable whose value determines whether the model succeeds on this item. An example is whether the attribute is retrieved into the residual stream at the layers where downstream computation reads it.
- **p** is a *proxy variable*: an item-level internal variable that correlates with m\* but can be separated from it. An example is a representation of how familiar an entity name is, which can be strong even when no attribute is retrievable.
- **τ(x)** stands for *type features* of the prompt: domain, phrasing, entity category, length, and so on.

Four hypotheses follow.

- **H1, Inherited allocation.** Reports depend on x only through features that predict human hedging, A_D(x). They are not keyed to any item-specific variable reflecting the model's own competence.
- **H2, Self-theory.** Reports depend on x through features that predict the model's own error rate *for prompts of that type*. Post-training on the model's errors can install such a function: "hedge on questions about minor nineteenth-century figures," learned because that is where this model has tended to fail. The report tracks a *dispositional* fact about the model (its competence profile) but not the occurrent state of the episode.
- **H3, Proxy monitoring.** Reports depend on p, an item-level internal variable that correlates with m\* but can be separated from it.
- **H4, Direct monitoring.** Reports depend on m\*, or on a readout that is counterfactually tied to m\* item by item.

**Placing the original dilemma.** The dilemma's "tracking" corresponds to H4, and perhaps H3. Its "trained" corresponds to H1. But the four hypotheses are defined by grain, and all four are compatible with the reporting disposition having been produced by training. H2 is *both* trained and tracking: it tracks a real property of the model, just not an occurrent one. A disposition is an internal fact, so even H2 delivers evidence about the model's internal constitution, of a coarse-grained kind. The only hypothesis on which allocation tells us nothing model-specific is H1.

**Where the objector's hypothesis sits.** The objector's "trained, not tracking" must be H1, or H2 read deflationarily. Read that way, H2 says the reports reflect only the statistical distribution of past errors over prompt types, not the episode at hand.

**Four tests.** These hypotheses make distinct predictions under the following designs.

**T1: Stratify on inherited allocation.** Estimate A_D(x) independently, for example from human judgments of how likely a typical person is to hedge, or from an observer model with no stake in the target's competence. Then, *within strata of constant A_D*, measure whether the target's hedges discriminate its own successes from its failures.

- H1 predicts zero within-stratum resolution.
- H2 through H4 predict positive within-stratum resolution, with H2's limited to whatever type features can capture.

The most informative strata are those where human difficulty and model difficulty come apart:

- **Tokenization-sensitive tasks**, such as counting the letters in a word. Human authors almost never hedge on these. Models fail on them often and unevenly.
- **Synthetic entities.** Fictitious entities can be introduced by fine-tuning with different numbers of exposures. The human corpus says nothing about them at all, so A_D is constant across them, while retrieval success varies with exposure.

If a model's hedges discriminate its own failures inside such a stratum, imitation of human authors cannot be the explanation. Those authors had no differential behaviour there to imitate.

**T2: Siblings and observers.** Take models trained on the *same* corpus but differing in random seed or scale. The corpus, and hence A_D, is held fixed exactly. Competence profiles differ at the level of individual items. Ask whether each sibling's allocation predicts *its own* item-level errors better than it predicts its sibling's.

- H1 predicts no self-advantage.

The observer variant is stronger. Train an observer model on the target's own input-output behaviour, so that it can learn the target's self-theory in H2's sense. Then ask whether the target predicts its own errors better than the observer does. Binder et al. (2024) report a design of this form for self-prediction, finding that models predict their own behaviour better than observer models trained on that behaviour. The logic is the same as Nisbett and Wilson's (1977) classic comparison of subjects' reports with those of observers asked to predict the subjects' behaviour, which I return to in §8.

- H2 predicts no self-advantage over a well-trained observer. A self-theory learned from behaviour is, in principle, available to anyone who sees the behaviour.
- H3 and H4 predict a self-advantage, because the target has access to item-level variables the observer cannot see.

**T3: Item-level intervention.** Alter the model's competence on a single item while holding the prompt, the item's type, and the corpus fixed. Possible tools include targeted knowledge editing (Meng et al. 2022), unlearning a specific fact, or fine-tuning one in.

- H1 and H2 predict that hedging on that item does not change, because nothing they key on has changed.
- H3 and H4 predict that hedging follows the competence change.

**T4: Proxy dissociation.** Intervene on m\* while sparing p, or on p while sparing m\*.

- H3 predicts that hedging follows p.
- H4 predicts that hedging follows m\*.

**What existing work suggests.** There is already some relevant evidence, though it is incomplete and specific to particular models.

- Kadavath et al. (2022) found that models can be trained to predict whether they know an answer, and that this generalizes somewhat across tasks. That is suggestive, but not decisive between H2 and H3–H4.
- Yona, Aharoni and Geva (2024) found that models' verbal decisiveness often fails to reflect their intrinsic uncertainty. That is evidence that, for the models studied, much verbal hedging is closer to H1 or to style.
- Ferrando et al. (2025) identified internal directions encoding whether an entity is recognized, and showed that steering them causally modulates refusal to answer.
- The circuit analyses in Lindsey et al. (2025a) describe a default "can't answer" pathway that is inhibited by features representing known entities. On their account, some hallucinations arise when the familiarity signal fires without the corresponding knowledge being available.

That is H3: allocation keyed to an item-level internal variable that can be separated from retrieval success. Whatever the generality of these findings, they show that the four hypotheses are not merely logically distinct. Interpretability methods can already tell them apart in at least some cases.

## 6. The common cause, examined

Now return to part (2) of the objection. Corpus frequency F causes the internal variable m\*. F also causes the hedge r, via imitation of humans who hedge on rare facts. So the correlation between m\* and r is said to be spurious, explained by F.

**Where the fork has to live.** There is an important asymmetry between this common-cause structure and the usual case in which a confounder is postulated. In a trained network, F has no causal access to r *except through the network's computation on x*. Corpus frequency is a fact about the training data. At inference, its influence is entirely encoded in weights and expressed through intermediate representations. So the claimed fork, F → m\* and F → r with no edge m\* → r, has to be realized *inside the network*. There must be two pathways from the input representation. One computes m\*. The other computes r. And the second does not read from the first.

**What the fork claim really is.** That is a substantive hypothesis about the network's internal causal structure. It is H1 (or H2) as a claim about mediation. The rival chain is F → m\* → r: frequency determines whether retrieval succeeds, and the reporting pathway reads whether retrieval succeeded. That is H4.

The objector speaks as if frequency's being a common cause were established by the observation that F influences both m\* and r. It is not. Both causal structures entail that F influences both. They differ in whether the influence on r is mediated by m\*. So "corpus frequency is a common cause" is not an alternative to the mediation question. It is one answer to it.

**How the tests break the common cause.** Each of the tests in §5 breaks the F-dependence in some way.

- **T1** chooses strata in which F, as it bears on *human* hedging, is constant or irrelevant, while model competence varies. On synthetic entities, human-corpus frequency is zero throughout.
- **T2** holds F exactly constant across siblings, while letting m\* vary through differences in seed or scale.
- **T3** changes m\* by direct intervention while F is unchanged. The corpus is not touched when a fact is edited out of the weights.
- **T4** goes beyond F and asks which internal variable carries the dependence.

None of these tests could turn out positive on the fork hypothesis. On each design, the common-cause story predicts a null. A positive result therefore discriminates between the hypotheses.

**An apparent counterexample.** One version of the fork survives T3. Suppose the network's hedge pathway reads a representation *shared* with retrieval, for instance a general entity-familiarity representation that both supports retrieval and feeds the hedge. Editing out a fact might degrade that shared representation and so move the hedge. Is this the common-cause story surviving the test?

It is not. If the hedge pathway reads a representation that participates in the first-order computation, then the hedge depends counterfactually on an item-level state of the model's own processing. That is H3 or H4, depending on whether the shared representation is m\* itself or a proxy for it. Sharing of representations is not a way of escaping tracking. It is one of the ways tracking is implemented.

What would genuinely vindicate the fork is a hedge pathway reading a representation *dedicated* to estimating human obscurity: one that does not participate in retrieval and that leaves the hedge unmoved by interventions on retrieval. That is exactly what T3 and T4 can detect.

## 7. The regression dilemma, conceded and replaced

Part (4) of the objection is the most methodologically precise, and its first horn is correct as aimed at the design my proposal originally described.

**Horn 1: conditioning on the full prompt.** Within a single fixed network, every internal variable is a deterministic function of x. An observational regression across prompts, within one network, that conditions on the full prompt leaves nothing to explain. And no observational regression within one network can separate x → m\* → r from a structure in which m\* and r are parallel functions of x. Both structures generate the same joint distribution over (x, m\*, r).

I accept this. Observational regression within a single network is the wrong instrument.

But the reason it fails shows what the right instrument is. The rival hypotheses are claims about *mediation*: about which intermediate variables carry the influence of x to r. Mediation is not identified by input–output behaviour. It is identified by intervention: holding the input fixed and setting the intermediate variable to a different value (Pearl 2009). In a biological organism such interventions are hard to perform. In a network they are routine. Standard techniques include:

- activation patching and causal mediation analysis (Vig et al. 2020);
- interchange interventions, which swap an internal variable's value between a run where the model succeeds and a run where it fails while the prompt is held fixed (Geiger et al. 2021).

That internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt is no obstacle to such analysis. A digital circuit is deterministic too, and whether its output depends on a given wire is settled by clamping that wire.

The first horn also misses a second source of variation. Comparison *across* networks (T2) supplies natural variation in m\* with x, and indeed the whole corpus, held fixed. The claim that "internal states have no residual variance given the prompt" is true within one network and false across siblings.

**Horn 2: conditioning on hand-picked features.** The second horn says that if we condition on a hand-picked set of surface features, residual covariance is guaranteed for any network richer than those features. There are three replies.

1. **The conditioning set is not arbitrary.** The right thing to hold fixed is the *rival hypothesis's own predictor*. For H1, that is an estimate of A_D(x). For H2, it is an observer model's prediction of the target's errors from behaviour. Conditioning on these is not conditioning on "surface features" chosen at will. It is conditioning on everything the deflationary hypothesis says drives allocation. If residual dependence remains, the deflationary hypothesis has failed by its own standard. The objector might respond that A_D and the observer's predictions can only be estimated imperfectly. That is true. But estimation error is not specific to any one variable, which leads to the second reply.

2. **Richness predicts residual covariance, but not specific residual covariance.** Generic richness guarantees that r has some residual covariance with *many* internal variables. Tracking makes a *specificity* prediction: the residual dependence should concentrate on m\* (or p), and interventions on internal variables of comparable richness that are irrelevant to first-order success should leave r unmoved. Two examples of irrelevant variables would be representations of a prompt's sentiment or register.

   Generic richness predicts no such pattern. If residual covariance were an artefact of richness alone, it would be spread across internal variables in proportion to their correlation with the unmodelled parts of x. It would not pick out the variable that governs whether the answer is correct. Two further checks sharpen the specificity prediction. The dependence should be monotone in the right direction: weaker retrieval should produce more hedging, not less. It should also respect the item-level structure that T3 exploits.

3. **The guarantee was about observation, not intervention.** The guarantee of residual covariance concerns observational covariance. It says nothing about whether an item-level intervention on m\* moves r. Richness of representation does not entail that hedging follows a targeted edit of one fact. That is a further, falsifiable claim.

**The off-manifold worry.** Interventions may put the network into states it never encounters naturally. Reports produced in those states might reflect a generic response to something anomalous rather than the specific variable intervened on. Lindsey's (2025b) experiments on injecting concept representations and asking models whether they notice anything raise exactly this issue. The worry is real. It recommends three things:

- preferring interventions that stay on the natural manifold, such as fine-tuning facts in or out, sibling variation, and interchange interventions that import a variable's value from a genuine run rather than an arbitrary vector;
- including controls that perturb irrelevant variables by comparable magnitudes;
- treating reports under off-manifold steering as weaker evidence.

None of this rescues the claim that the hypotheses cannot be distinguished.

**Summary.** The first horn defeats one design, which I abandon. The second horn shows only that observational residuals are insufficient, and specificity and intervention go beyond observational residuals. Neither horn shows that a positive result is predicted by "trained, not tracking," provided that slogan is cashed out as H1 or deflationary H2. Positive results on T1 through T4 are predicted by neither.

## 8. What allocation evidence delivers, and what it does not

Suppose the tests come back positive, at least for some report types in some models. Here is what would have been established.

**Reference and description come apart.** Allocation fixes what a report is *keyed to*. Lexicon fixes how the report *describes* it. Take "I'm not certain I remember." Suppose its allocation passes T3 for retrieval failure: it appears when, and because, a fact fails to be retrieved. Then the report is a reliable indicator of retrieval failure. But its lexical content, inherited from human speakers, describes that state as a lapse of memory with an experiential or episodic character that the system may lack.

So a report can be a good indicator and a poor description at the same time. This is why critiques aimed only at the lexicon ("it just uses human words") miss their target. They are critiques of description, and the evidential question concerns indication. Conversely, passing the allocation tests does not vindicate the lexicon. The proper inference from a well-allocated "I'm not certain I remember" is "retrieval failed," not "the system has a feeling of fading memory."

**Proxy monitoring is the human standard, not a deficiency.** If the evidence favours H3, as the familiarity-circuit findings suggest for at least some refusals, one might conclude that the model does not "really" monitor its knowledge. But human metacognition is substantially proxy-based.

- Reder and Ritter (1992) found that people's initial feeling of knowing is driven by familiarity with the terms of the question rather than with the answer.
- Koriat's (1993) accessibility account holds that feelings of knowing are based on the amount and ease of partial information retrieved, whether or not that information is correct.

These are paradigm H3 structures. Human reports of knowing are keyed to internal variables that correlate with, and can be separated from, the first-order variable, and they misfire systematically when the two come apart. The tip-of-the-tongue experience for a familiar face whose name one never learned is an example. We do not conclude that human feelings of knowing carry no information about human internal states. We conclude that they carry information about *familiarity* and *accessibility*, and through those, imperfectly, about knowledge. The same conclusion would hold for a model.

**Confabulation is H1 or H2, and the remedy is old.** Nisbett and Wilson's (1977) evidence that people's explanations of their own behaviour often match the predictions of observers is, in present terms, evidence that those explanations are allocated by a self-theory or a culturally inherited theory rather than by monitoring. Schwitzgebel (2008) argues that naive introspection about even current conscious experience is unreliable in related ways. So the human case contains every grain the four hypotheses distinguish, and which grain a given report has is settled by observer and intervention designs. This is not a double standard. It is the same standard applied with better instruments, since networks allow interventions that brains do not.

**Evidence is per report type, not wholesale.** The allocation thesis does not license a general verdict on whether "model self-reports" are evidence. Expressions of factual uncertainty may be keyed to retrieval-related variables. "This is confusing" may be keyed to nothing more specific than the inherited allocation of human confusion talk. Reports of affect may have no well-defined first-order variable to be keyed to at all. Each predicate needs its own m\* and its own tests. Where no candidate m\* can be specified, the allocation thesis does not yield a positive verdict. It yields the conclusion that the report's evidential standing is unestablished.

**Functional, not phenomenal.** Allocation evidence concerns functional internal states, such as retrieval success, entropy, and familiarity. It does not settle whether any of these states is conscious. On the gaming problem as Birch poses it for sentience, the result is partial. It shows how the problem can be answered for functional states despite training on human reports. It shows that the bare fact of training does not settle the matter. And it identifies which reports could even be candidates for further evidential use. It does not close the further gap between functional and phenomenal states, and nothing here pretends otherwise.

## 9. Does the dilemma reappear?

The objection concludes that the dilemma "is not dissolved; it reappears at the level of allocation." In one sense this is right. One can still ask, of the allocation of a given report, whether it is inherited or keyed to the model's states. But the dilemma's force came from its disjuncts being exclusive and exhaustive, and from the presumption that being trained settles the matter against tracking. At the level of allocation, neither feature survives.

**Not exclusive.** H3 and H4 can be produced by training, whether by pretraining using the model's own state as a proxy for human obscurity (§3) or by post-training on the model's own errors (§4). Being trained is compatible with tracking at the finest grain.

**Not exhaustive.** H2 is neither pure imitation nor occurrent monitoring. It is tracking of dispositional self-facts. H3 is tracking of an internal state other than the one the lexicon names. A binary verdict misdescribes both.

**Aetiology does not decide.** The question that matters for evidence, which variable the report counterfactually depends on, is not answered by learning how the reporting disposition came to exist. It is answered by T1 through T4.

So what replaces the dilemma is a classification problem with at least four answers. Each answer has known signatures under designs that hold the corpus, the prompt, or both fixed while varying the model's states. The original proposal said: trained in lexicon, tracking in allocation. The refined proposal says that training on human reports fixes the lexicon and the inherited allocation, A_D. Training on the model's own performance, or the instrumental use of its own states in imitation, may or may not add dependence on model-specific variables. Whether it has done so, and on which variables, is an empirical question about causal grain.

The objection was right that the original regression could not answer that question. It was wrong that no design could. The objection's own premise, that internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt, is what makes interventional designs possible.

# Trained in Lexicon, Keyed in Allocation: Language-Model Self-Reports and the Common-Cause Objection

## 1. The dilemma and a proposal

Large language models produce sentences such as "I'm not sure," "this is confusing," and "I'm not certain I remember." These are self-reports in grammatical form. The question is whether they are evidence about the internal states of the system that produces them.

A familiar worry says they are not. The models are trained on enormous corpora of human self-reports, so they would produce such sentences whether or not anything inside them corresponds to what the sentences describe. Birch (2024) calls the general version of this the *gaming problem*: behavioural markers that would be evidence of a state in an animal lose their evidential force in a system optimized to reproduce those markers. Perez and Long (2023) make a parallel point about self-reports specifically. The worry is usually posed as a dilemma. Either a model's report is *trained*, and so evidentially idle, or it is *tracking*, and so evidence of the state it reports. Since every report a model produces is trained in some sense, the dilemma seems to resolve in the deflationist's favour.

The proposal I defend splits self-report behaviour into two components.

- **Lexicon** is the repertoire of predicates a model uses and their phrasing.
- **Allocation** is the mapping from particular episodes to particular predicates: which forward passes are followed by "I'm unsure" and which are not.

Training on human reports clearly explains the lexicon. The proposal is that it does not explain allocation. Allocation is where evidence about internal states lives. Suppose allocation covaries with independently measured internal variables, such as output entropy, retrieval failure, or the activation of particular features, beyond what prompt-level predictors explain. Then that covariance needs a mechanism, and imitation of humans does not supply one. A report can be trained in its lexicon and tracking in its allocation, so the dilemma dissolves.

## 2. The Common-Cause Objection

A strong objection says this proposal fails at its central premise. It has four parts.

1. **No split.** A next-token predictor is not given a repertoire and then left to allocate it. Training fits the whole conditional distribution P(report | context), and that distribution already encodes allocation. Human corpora record *when* people say "I'm unsure": on obscure questions, ambiguous questions, and questions about rare entities.
2. **Common cause.** The model's internal variables are not independent of this. Entropy and retrieval failure are learned functions of the same inputs, driven by the same corpus statistics, notably how often the queried fact appears in training (Kandpal et al. 2023). Corpus frequency is therefore a common cause of the internal variable and of the imitated hedge.
3. **Post-training supplies the mechanism.** Reinforcement learning from human feedback, honesty fine-tuning, and calibration training (e.g. Lin, Hilton and Evans 2022) reward hedging on the model's own errors. They train allocation directly on the model's forward passes, so the "missing mechanism" is not missing.
4. **The test cannot discriminate.** Internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt.
   - If "prompt-level predictors" means the full prompt, the internal variables have no residual variance left to explain anything.
   - If it means a hand-picked set of surface features, residual covariance is guaranteed for any network whose representations are richer than those features.
   - Either way, a positive result is predicted by "trained, not tracking." The dilemma reappears at the level of allocation.

I think the objection is right about several things, and I concede them below:

- The proposal as first stated overstates what the corpus fails to fix.
- The regression design as first stated is inadequate.
- Post-training does supply a mechanism.

But the objection's conclusion does not follow. Properly developed, the objection's own premises sharpen the original idea rather than refute it.

The revised thesis I will argue for is this. Training on human reports explains the lexicon and one specific component of allocation, which I call *inherited allocation*. Evidence about internal states lives in a different component: the counterfactual dependence of allocation on model-specific variables once inherited allocation is held fixed. That dependence is identified by comparative and interventional designs, not by observational regression within a single network. Its aetiology, including post-training on the model's own errors, does not compete with its evidential import. The question "trained or tracking?" is replaced by a question about *causal grain*. That question has more than two answers, and they can be told apart.

## 3. What the corpus fixes: inherited allocation

Start with part (1). The objector is right that pretraining fits a conditional distribution that includes something deserving the name "allocation." The question is *which* allocation, and the answer follows from what a human corpus records.

**What the corpus records.** Consider contexts x in which a speaker is asked something and may hedge. The process that generates the human corpus D involves three things:

- the context x;
- the epistemic state s of the human author who confronts x;
- the report r the author produces.

Only x and r are written down. The author's state is not.

**What pretraining converges to.** A model trained to optimality on D therefore converges toward

> P_D(r | x) = Σ_s P_D(r | x, s) · P_D(s | x).

This expression has two features that matter.

1. It is a function of x alone.
2. Its dependence on x runs through P_D(s | x), the probability that a typical author confronting x is in a hedging state.

Call A_D(x) = P_D(hedge | x) the *inherited allocation*. It is the hedge rate appropriate to the population of human authors who might have written a continuation of x. The objector is right that the corpus fixes A_D. The objector is also right that A_D correlates with obscurity, ambiguity, and rarity, since those are what put human authors into hedging states.

**What the corpus leaves out.** The model's own state never appears in this derivation. Call that state m: for a factual query, whether the relevant attribute is actually retrieved in the model's forward pass. The corpus contains no term for m. So inherited allocation is not allocation over the model's forward passes in the sense my proposal needed. It is allocation over *prompts*, at the rate fitting a typical human. Two systems with identical A_D but different competence profiles would, as pure imitators, hedge identically. One of them would then hedge on things it knows, and the other would answer confidently things it does not know.

So the lexicon/allocation split survives, in a refined form. The corpus determines the lexicon and A_D. It does not determine whether, and how, reports depend on m beyond their dependence on x. The original claim that "the corpus does not say on which of the model's own forward passes to deploy each phrase" was too quick: the corpus says a great deal about when to deploy each phrase, but only for a typical human author. The correct claim is narrower. Whatever the corpus says about allocation, it says through A_D.

**A twist in the objector's favour, which turns out not to be.** Pretraining could itself make reports depend on m. A model trying to predict whether a human author would hedge on x needs an estimate of how obscure x is. One excellent cue to obscurity is the model's own difficulty in answering. If retrieval fails, the fact is probably rare, and a human writing about it probably hedged. A good imitator therefore has reason to use m as an input to its hedge prediction.

This looks like grist for the objector: a purely imitative objective can wire the internal variable into the hedge. But consider what it implies.

- If pretraining makes r depend on m, then r *does* carry information about m, even though the system was optimized to predict humans, not to report on itself.
- It also makes a distinctive prediction. On items where human obscurity and model competence come apart, such a system will follow m. It will be a *worse* imitator of humans and a *better* indicator of itself.

The twist therefore does not support "trained, not tracking." It shows that the training objective does not settle what the report depends on. That brings us to the issue on which the whole debate turns.

## 4. Aetiology is not grain

The dilemma "trained or tracking?" treats the two options as rivals. They are rivals only if the fact that a reporting disposition was produced by training excludes, or undercuts, its counterfactual dependence on the state reported. Nothing supports that assumption.

**What evidence requires.** A report is evidence about a state to the extent that observing it should change our credence about the state. It is robust evidence to the extent that the report counterfactually depends on the state, so that intervening on the state would change the report (Dretske 1981; Woodward 2003). Facts about *why* this dependence exists, such as an engineer's calibration, natural selection, or a gradient, do not cancel the dependence. Two examples make the point.

- **The thermometer.** A thermometer calibrated against a reference instrument is not shown to be untrustworthy by the discovery that it was calibrated. Calibration is what makes it trustworthy.
- **The child.** A child learns to say "I don't know" from caregivers who respond to the child's actual performance. The caregivers praise honest admissions and correct confident errors. That is, structurally, post-training on the learner's own errors. No one infers that the child's "I don't know" is trained and therefore not tracking. The training explains how the tracking was installed.

**What this does to part (3) of the objection.** Post-training that rewards hedging on the model's own errors does supply a mechanism for allocation. But it is not the mechanism my proposal denied the corpus could supply. The proposal concerned training on *human* reports. Post-training on the model's own errors is a different process, and it is precisely the kind of process that installs dependence on the model's own states. A reward that depends on the model's own correctness can only be maximized by a policy whose reports depend on something correlated with its own correctness. That something is either the state that determines correctness or a proxy for it.

So the objection's third part is not a defeater. It is a candidate *explanation* of tracking. The proposal should have said so from the start.

**Separating calibration from resolution.** The post-training point does have a residue worth keeping. Some post-training effects do not touch allocation at all. A reward model that prefers hedged prose shifts the *base rate* of hedging. Such a shift can improve aggregate calibration while leaving the item-by-item pattern of hedges unchanged.

The forecasting literature has the right tools here. Murphy (1973) decomposed the probability score into three parts:

- **reliability**, the match between stated confidence and observed frequency;
- **resolution**, the ability to give different forecasts on occasions with different outcomes;
- **uncertainty**, the base-rate difficulty of the task.

A forecaster who always predicts the base rate is perfectly calibrated and has zero resolution. Allocation evidence is a matter of resolution, not calibration. A model's overall hedge rate is a lexical-stylistic fact. Its *discrimination* between the episodes it gets right and the episodes it gets wrong is the allocation fact.

**The real question.** Once aetiology is separated from dependence, "trained, not tracking" cannot simply mean "this was produced by training." It must be a claim about causal grain: the claim that allocation is keyed to variables *other than* the state the report is taken to be about. That is a substantive empirical hypothesis. It comes in several versions, and they make different predictions.

## 5. Four hypotheses about causal grain

Fix a class of reports, say expressions of uncertainty about factual queries. Distinguish three kinds of variable the report might depend on.

- **m\*** is the *first-order variable*: the internal variable whose value determines whether the model succeeds on this item. An example is whether the attribute is retrieved into the residual stream at the layers where downstream computation reads it.
- **p** is a *proxy variable*: an item-level internal variable that correlates with m\* but can be separated from it. An example is a representation of how familiar an entity name is, which can be strong even when no attribute is retrievable.
- **τ(x)** stands for *type features* of the prompt: domain, phrasing, entity category, length, and so on.

Four hypotheses follow.

- **H1, Inherited allocation.** Reports depend on x only through features that predict human hedging, A_D(x). They are not keyed to any item-specific variable reflecting the model's own competence.
- **H2, Self-theory.** Reports depend on x through features that predict the model's own error rate *for prompts of that type*. Post-training on the model's errors can install such a function: "hedge on questions about minor nineteenth-century figures," learned because that is where this model has tended to fail. The report tracks a *dispositional* fact about the model (its competence profile) but not the occurrent state of the episode.
- **H3, Proxy monitoring.** Reports depend on p, an item-level internal variable that correlates with m\* but can be separated from it.
- **H4, Direct monitoring.** Reports depend on m\*, or on a readout that is counterfactually tied to m\* item by item.

**Placing the original dilemma.** The dilemma's "tracking" corresponds to H4, and perhaps H3. Its "trained" corresponds to H1. But the four hypotheses are defined by grain, and all four are compatible with the reporting disposition having been produced by training. H2 is *both* trained and tracking: it tracks a real property of the model, just not an occurrent one. A disposition is an internal fact, so even H2 delivers evidence about the model's internal constitution, of a coarse-grained kind. The only hypothesis on which allocation tells us nothing model-specific is H1.

**Where the objector's hypothesis sits.** The objector's "trained, not tracking" must be H1, or H2 read deflationarily. Read that way, H2 says the reports reflect only the statistical distribution of past errors over prompt types, not the episode at hand.

**Four tests.** These hypotheses make distinct predictions under the following designs.

**T1: Stratify on inherited allocation.** Estimate A_D(x) independently, for example from human judgments of how likely a typical person is to hedge, or from an observer model with no stake in the target's competence. Then, *within strata of constant A_D*, measure whether the target's hedges discriminate its own successes from its failures.

- H1 predicts zero within-stratum resolution.
- H2 through H4 predict positive within-stratum resolution, with H2's limited to whatever type features can capture.

The most informative strata are those where human difficulty and model difficulty come apart:

- **Tokenization-sensitive tasks**, such as counting the letters in a word. Human authors almost never hedge on these. Models fail on them often and unevenly.
- **Synthetic entities.** Fictitious entities can be introduced by fine-tuning with different numbers of exposures. The human corpus says nothing about them at all, so A_D is constant across them, while retrieval success varies with exposure.

If a model's hedges discriminate its own failures inside such a stratum, imitation of human authors cannot be the explanation. Those authors had no differential behaviour there to imitate.

**T2: Siblings and observers.** Take models trained on the *same* corpus but differing in random seed or scale. The corpus, and hence A_D, is held fixed exactly. Competence profiles differ at the level of individual items. Ask whether each sibling's allocation predicts *its own* item-level errors better than it predicts its sibling's.

- H1 predicts no self-advantage.

The observer variant is stronger. Train an observer model on the target's own input-output behaviour, so that it can learn the target's self-theory in H2's sense. Then ask whether the target predicts its own errors better than the observer does. Binder et al. (2024) report a design of this form for self-prediction, finding that models predict their own behaviour better than observer models trained on that behaviour. The logic is the same as Nisbett and Wilson's (1977) classic comparison of subjects' reports with those of observers asked to predict the subjects' behaviour, which I return to in §8.

- H2 predicts no self-advantage over a well-trained observer. A self-theory learned from behaviour is, in principle, available to anyone who sees the behaviour.
- H3 and H4 predict a self-advantage, because the target has access to item-level variables the observer cannot see.

**T3: Item-level intervention.** Alter the model's competence on a single item while holding the prompt, the item's type, and the corpus fixed. Possible tools include targeted knowledge editing (Meng et al. 2022), unlearning a specific fact, or fine-tuning one in.

- H1 and H2 predict that hedging on that item does not change, because nothing they key on has changed.
- H3 and H4 predict that hedging follows the competence change.

**T4: Proxy dissociation.** Intervene on m\* while sparing p, or on p while sparing m\*.

- H3 predicts that hedging follows p.
- H4 predicts that hedging follows m\*.

**What existing work suggests.** There is already some relevant evidence, though it is incomplete and specific to particular models.

- Kadavath et al. (2022) found that models can be trained to predict whether they know an answer, and that this generalizes somewhat across tasks. That is suggestive, but not decisive between H2 and H3–H4.
- Yona, Aharoni and Geva (2024) found that models' verbal decisiveness often fails to reflect their intrinsic uncertainty. That is evidence that, for the models studied, much verbal hedging is closer to H1 or to style.
- Ferrando et al. (2025) identified internal directions encoding whether an entity is recognized, and showed that steering them causally modulates refusal to answer.
- The circuit analyses in Lindsey et al. (2025a) describe a default "can't answer" pathway that is inhibited by features representing known entities. On their account, some hallucinations arise when the familiarity signal fires without the corresponding knowledge being available.

That is H3: allocation keyed to an item-level internal variable that can be separated from retrieval success. Whatever the generality of these findings, they show that the four hypotheses are not merely logically distinct. Interpretability methods can already tell them apart in at least some cases.

## 6. The common cause, examined

Now return to part (2) of the objection. Corpus frequency F causes the internal variable m\*. F also causes the hedge r, via imitation of humans who hedge on rare facts. So the correlation between m\* and r is said to be spurious, explained by F.

**Where the fork has to live.** There is an important asymmetry between this common-cause structure and the usual case in which a confounder is postulated. In a trained network, F has no causal access to r *except through the network's computation on x*. Corpus frequency is a fact about the training data. At inference, its influence is entirely encoded in weights and expressed through intermediate representations. So the claimed fork, F → m\* and F → r with no edge m\* → r, has to be realized *inside the network*. There must be two pathways from the input representation. One computes m\*. The other computes r. And the second does not read from the first.

**What the fork claim really is.** That is a substantive hypothesis about the network's internal causal structure. It is H1 (or H2) as a claim about mediation. The rival chain is F → m\* → r: frequency determines whether retrieval succeeds, and the reporting pathway reads whether retrieval succeeded. That is H4.

The objector speaks as if frequency's being a common cause were established by the observation that F influences both m\* and r. It is not. Both causal structures entail that F influences both. They differ in whether the influence on r is mediated by m\*. So "corpus frequency is a common cause" is not an alternative to the mediation question. It is one answer to it.

**How the tests break the common cause.** Each of the tests in §5 breaks the F-dependence in some way.

- **T1** chooses strata in which F, as it bears on *human* hedging, is constant or irrelevant, while model competence varies. On synthetic entities, human-corpus frequency is zero throughout.
- **T2** holds F exactly constant across siblings, while letting m\* vary through differences in seed or scale.
- **T3** changes m\* by direct intervention while F is unchanged. The corpus is not touched when a fact is edited out of the weights.
- **T4** goes beyond F and asks which internal variable carries the dependence.

None of these tests could turn out positive on the fork hypothesis. On each design, the common-cause story predicts a null. A positive result therefore discriminates between the hypotheses.

**An apparent counterexample.** One version of the fork survives T3. Suppose the network's hedge pathway reads a representation *shared* with retrieval, for instance a general entity-familiarity representation that both supports retrieval and feeds the hedge. Editing out a fact might degrade that shared representation and so move the hedge. Is this the common-cause story surviving the test?

It is not. If the hedge pathway reads a representation that participates in the first-order computation, then the hedge depends counterfactually on an item-level state of the model's own processing. That is H3 or H4, depending on whether the shared representation is m\* itself or a proxy for it. Sharing of representations is not a way of escaping tracking. It is one of the ways tracking is implemented.

What would genuinely vindicate the fork is a hedge pathway reading a representation *dedicated* to estimating human obscurity: one that does not participate in retrieval and that leaves the hedge unmoved by interventions on retrieval. That is exactly what T3 and T4 can detect.

## 7. The regression dilemma, conceded and replaced

Part (4) of the objection is the most methodologically precise, and its first horn is correct as aimed at the design my proposal originally described.

**Horn 1: conditioning on the full prompt.** Within a single fixed network, every internal variable is a deterministic function of x. An observational regression across prompts, within one network, that conditions on the full prompt leaves nothing to explain. And no observational regression within one network can separate x → m\* → r from a structure in which m\* and r are parallel functions of x. Both structures generate the same joint distribution over (x, m\*, r).

I accept this. Observational regression within a single network is the wrong instrument.

But the reason it fails shows what the right instrument is. The rival hypotheses are claims about *mediation*: about which intermediate variables carry the influence of x to r. Mediation is not identified by input–output behaviour. It is identified by intervention: holding the input fixed and setting the intermediate variable to a different value (Pearl 2009). In a biological organism such interventions are hard to perform. In a network they are routine. Standard techniques include:

- activation patching and causal mediation analysis (Vig et al. 2020);
- interchange interventions, which swap an internal variable's value between a run where the model succeeds and a run where it fails while the prompt is held fixed (Geiger et al. 2021).

That internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt is no obstacle to such analysis. A digital circuit is deterministic too, and whether its output depends on a given wire is settled by clamping that wire.

The first horn also misses a second source of variation. Comparison *across* networks (T2) supplies natural variation in m\* with x, and indeed the whole corpus, held fixed. The claim that "internal states have no residual variance given the prompt" is true within one network and false across siblings.

**Horn 2: conditioning on hand-picked features.** The second horn says that if we condition on a hand-picked set of surface features, residual covariance is guaranteed for any network richer than those features. There are three replies.

1. **The conditioning set is not arbitrary.** The right thing to hold fixed is the *rival hypothesis's own predictor*. For H1, that is an estimate of A_D(x). For H2, it is an observer model's prediction of the target's errors from behaviour. Conditioning on these is not conditioning on "surface features" chosen at will. It is conditioning on everything the deflationary hypothesis says drives allocation. If residual dependence remains, the deflationary hypothesis has failed by its own standard. The objector might respond that A_D and the observer's predictions can only be estimated imperfectly. That is true. But estimation error is not specific to any one variable, which leads to the second reply.

2. **Richness predicts residual covariance, but not specific residual covariance.** Generic richness guarantees that r has some residual covariance with *many* internal variables. Tracking makes a *specificity* prediction: the residual dependence should concentrate on m\* (or p), and interventions on internal variables of comparable richness that are irrelevant to first-order success should leave r unmoved. Two examples of irrelevant variables would be representations of a prompt's sentiment or register.

   Generic richness predicts no such pattern. If residual covariance were an artefact of richness alone, it would be spread across internal variables in proportion to their correlation with the unmodelled parts of x. It would not pick out the variable that governs whether the answer is correct. Two further checks sharpen the specificity prediction. The dependence should be monotone in the right direction: weaker retrieval should produce more hedging, not less. It should also respect the item-level structure that T3 exploits.

3. **The guarantee was about observation, not intervention.** The guarantee of residual covariance concerns observational covariance. It says nothing about whether an item-level intervention on m\* moves r. Richness of representation does not entail that hedging follows a targeted edit of one fact. That is a further, falsifiable claim.

**The off-manifold worry.** Interventions may put the network into states it never encounters naturally. Reports produced in those states might reflect a generic response to something anomalous rather than the specific variable intervened on. Lindsey's (2025b) experiments on injecting concept representations and asking models whether they notice anything raise exactly this issue. The worry is real. It recommends three things:

- preferring interventions that stay on the natural manifold, such as fine-tuning facts in or out, sibling variation, and interchange interventions that import a variable's value from a genuine run rather than an arbitrary vector;
- including controls that perturb irrelevant variables by comparable magnitudes;
- treating reports under off-manifold steering as weaker evidence.

None of this rescues the claim that the hypotheses cannot be distinguished.

**Summary.** The first horn defeats one design, which I abandon. The second horn shows only that observational residuals are insufficient, and specificity and intervention go beyond observational residuals. Neither horn shows that a positive result is predicted by "trained, not tracking," provided that slogan is cashed out as H1 or deflationary H2. Positive results on T1 through T4 are predicted by neither.

## 8. What allocation evidence delivers, and what it does not

Suppose the tests come back positive, at least for some report types in some models. Here is what would have been established.

**Reference and description come apart.** Allocation fixes what a report is *keyed to*. Lexicon fixes how the report *describes* it. Take "I'm not certain I remember." Suppose its allocation passes T3 for retrieval failure: it appears when, and because, a fact fails to be retrieved. Then the report is a reliable indicator of retrieval failure. But its lexical content, inherited from human speakers, describes that state as a lapse of memory with an experiential or episodic character that the system may lack.

So a report can be a good indicator and a poor description at the same time. This is why critiques aimed only at the lexicon ("it just uses human words") miss their target. They are critiques of description, and the evidential question concerns indication. Conversely, passing the allocation tests does not vindicate the lexicon. The proper inference from a well-allocated "I'm not certain I remember" is "retrieval failed," not "the system has a feeling of fading memory."

**Proxy monitoring is the human standard, not a deficiency.** If the evidence favours H3, as the familiarity-circuit findings suggest for at least some refusals, one might conclude that the model does not "really" monitor its knowledge. But human metacognition is substantially proxy-based.

- Reder and Ritter (1992) found that people's initial feeling of knowing is driven by familiarity with the terms of the question rather than with the answer.
- Koriat's (1993) accessibility account holds that feelings of knowing are based on the amount and ease of partial information retrieved, whether or not that information is correct.

These are paradigm H3 structures. Human reports of knowing are keyed to internal variables that correlate with, and can be separated from, the first-order variable, and they misfire systematically when the two come apart. The tip-of-the-tongue experience for a familiar face whose name one never learned is an example. We do not conclude that human feelings of knowing carry no information about human internal states. We conclude that they carry information about *familiarity* and *accessibility*, and through those, imperfectly, about knowledge. The same conclusion would hold for a model.

**Confabulation is H1 or H2, and the remedy is old.** Nisbett and Wilson's (1977) evidence that people's explanations of their own behaviour often match the predictions of observers is, in present terms, evidence that those explanations are allocated by a self-theory or a culturally inherited theory rather than by monitoring. Schwitzgebel (2008) argues that naive introspection about even current conscious experience is unreliable in related ways. So the human case contains every grain the four hypotheses distinguish, and which grain a given report has is settled by observer and intervention designs. This is not a double standard. It is the same standard applied with better instruments, since networks allow interventions that brains do not.

**Evidence is per report type, not wholesale.** The allocation thesis does not license a general verdict on whether "model self-reports" are evidence. Expressions of factual uncertainty may be keyed to retrieval-related variables. "This is confusing" may be keyed to nothing more specific than the inherited allocation of human confusion talk. Reports of affect may have no well-defined first-order variable to be keyed to at all. Each predicate needs its own m\* and its own tests. Where no candidate m\* can be specified, the allocation thesis does not yield a positive verdict. It yields the conclusion that the report's evidential standing is unestablished.

**Functional, not phenomenal.** Allocation evidence concerns functional internal states, such as retrieval success, entropy, and familiarity. It does not settle whether any of these states is conscious. On the gaming problem as Birch poses it for sentience, the result is partial. It shows how the problem can be answered for functional states despite training on human reports. It shows that the bare fact of training does not settle the matter. And it identifies which reports could even be candidates for further evidential use. It does not close the further gap between functional and phenomenal states, and nothing here pretends otherwise.

## 9. Does the dilemma reappear?

The objection concludes that the dilemma "is not dissolved; it reappears at the level of allocation." In one sense this is right. One can still ask, of the allocation of a given report, whether it is inherited or keyed to the model's states. But the dilemma's force came from its disjuncts being exclusive and exhaustive, and from the presumption that being trained settles the matter against tracking. At the level of allocation, neither feature survives.

**Not exclusive.** H3 and H4 can be produced by training, whether by pretraining using the model's own state as a proxy for human obscurity (§3) or by post-training on the model's own errors (§4). Being trained is compatible with tracking at the finest grain.

**Not exhaustive.** H2 is neither pure imitation nor occurrent monitoring. It is tracking of dispositional self-facts. H3 is tracking of an internal state other than the one the lexicon names. A binary verdict misdescribes both.

**Aetiology does not decide.** The question that matters for evidence, which variable the report counterfactually depends on, is not answered by learning how the reporting disposition came to exist. It is answered by T1 through T4.

So what replaces the dilemma is a classification problem with at least four answers. Each answer has known signatures under designs that hold the corpus, the prompt, or both fixed while varying the model's states. The original proposal said: trained in lexicon, tracking in allocation. The refined proposal says that training on human reports fixes the lexicon and the inherited allocation, A_D. Training on the model's own performance, or the instrumental use of its own states in imitation, may or may not add dependence on model-specific variables. Whether it has done so, and on which variables, is an empirical question about causal grain.

The objection was right that the original regression could not answer that question. It was wrong that no design could. The objection's own premise, that internal states are deterministic functions of the prompt, is what makes interventional designs possible.
